title: System DLL loaded from a user-writable path
why: DLL search-order hijacking. Written from a Sysmon lab where a copied calc.exe loaded a planted WININET.dll.

title: .NET runtime loaded by a process that is not a .NET host
why: Unmanaged PowerShell: the CLR injected into a native process so PowerShell runs with no powershell.exe in the process log.

title: SSH password brute force from one source
why: Ten failed passwords from one address in five minutes, as a Sigma correlation rule. Ported from my log triage tool.

title: Client bypassing the filtering resolver with encrypted DNS
why: A device looks up a DNS-over-HTTPS or Private Relay bootstrap host, after which the resolver stops seeing it. Written after it happened on my own network.

title: Systemd unit written outside a package manager
why: A new service or timer unit appears, written by something that is not a package manager or systemd. Units are the usual way to survive a reboot on Linux. I write them by hand on my own server, so I know the normal noise: rare, and always an editor or a shell.

techniques.name: Create or modify system process: systemd service

title: Container started with host-level access
why: A container asks to be privileged, to mount the Docker socket, or to share the host's process or network namespace. Any of these turns code in a container into code on the host. I run 40+ containers and know which few legitimately need it.

title: SSH authorized_keys modified outside SSH tooling
why: Adding a key is the quietest way to keep access to a Linux host: no password change, no new account, and it survives a reboot.

title: Sudoers written outside visudo or a package manager
why: One line in /etc/sudoers.d is a permanent route to root. Almost nothing legitimate writes there except visudo and package installs.

techniques.name: Abuse elevation control: sudo and sudo caching

title: Download piped straight into a shell
why: curl piped into sh is how many installers work and how most Linux first stages work, because the payload never touches the disk. On a server that is already built it should be rare enough to review.

techniques.name: Command and scripting interpreter: Unix shell

title: DNS query with a very long label
why: Tools that move data over DNS pack it into labels of up to 63 characters. People do not type 50-character hostnames, so long labels are what tunnelling looks like in a resolver log.
